identified_claims.claim_text: The final linear readability formula is Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 − 0.7295, where coefficients are the averages over 5 cross-validation folds.
evidence: Equation 16 presents the formula and Table 3 lists per-fold coefficient values whose mean matches the reported coefficients.
uncertainty_flags: No standard errors, p-values, or confidence intervals for coefficients provided; significance of coefficients is unknown.
No model diagnostics (residuals, heteroscedasticity, normality) reported to validate OLS assumptions.

identified_claims.claim_text: Under 5-fold cross-validation with rounding predicted continuous scores to the nearest integer class, the formula achieves average overall accuracy ~81% (per-fold overall accuracies: 78.39%, 81.50%, 83.42%, 80.40%, 80.90%), and per-class average accuracies around: Easy 76.6%, Normal 85.7%, Difficult 78.45%.
evidence: Table 3 reports per-fold and average accuracies for Easy/Normal/Difficult and Overall; text states 'Overall, the formula can predict ... with the accuracy up to 81%.'
CV setup described: 5 equal parts, 4 for training, 1 for testing, predicted values rounded to nearest integer.
uncertainty_flags: Rounding continuous scores to integer classes is an unexamined operational choice; boundary effects and calibration not analysed.
No per-fold confusion matrices, precision/recall/F1, or confidence intervals for accuracy provided.
No external or domain-separated test set; within-corpus CV may overestimate performance if data is not i.i.d. across sources/genres.

identified_claims.claim_text: Frequent-word lists derived from general newspaper corpora (Dinh and Hao) correlate poorly with readability in this dataset, so corpus-specific 'easy' lists are more effective for PDW-based features.
evidence: Table 2: PDW1 and PDS1 show low correlations with TR (PDW1=0.103, PDS1=0.051) while PDW2=0.786 and PDS2=0.466.
Discussion notes Dien and Hao lists are primarily from newspapers (mostly normal readability) hence mismatch.
uncertainty_flags: Comparison is limited to correlation values; no model-level ablation (training with PDW1 instead of PDW2) is reported to quantify downstream effect.
PDW2's derivation from easy documents of the same corpus risks circularity—superior correlation may reflect sampling artifacts.
Cross-domain performance or use of external easy-word lists is not tested.

identified_claims.claim_text: ASLS/ASLC (sentence length), AWLS/AWLC (word length), and PDW2 have strong positive correlations with human-assigned text readability (TR) in the corpus; some features are highly correlated with each other (e.g., ASLS~ASLC, AWLS~AWLC, ASLC~AWLC).
evidence: Table 2 correlation coefficients: TR with ASLC = 0.695, AWLC = 0.774, PDW2 = 0.786; ASLS-ASLC = 0.997, AWLS-AWLC = 0.979, ASLC-AWLC = 0.716.
uncertainty_flags: No hypothesis tests or significance levels are reported for correlations.
High inter-feature correlations suggest multicollinearity; the selection procedure uses an ad-hoc 0.9 threshold rather than established diagnostics (VIF).

identified_claims.claim_text: The formula is simple, interpretable, and can be applied in practice to predict Vietnamese text readability with high accuracy using easily computed surface features.
evidence: Abstract and conclusion make practical applicability claims and Table 3 shows reasonable within-corpus accuracies.
Features are simple to compute: character and word counts and a frequent-word list.
uncertainty_flags: Practical application presumes access to the corpus-derived easy-word list or an equivalent; portability of that list is untested.
No external validation or domain robustness checks presented to support broader applicability.

strengths.title: Substantially larger annotated Vietnamese corpus
strengths.description: The authors collected and curated a corpus of near 1,000 Vietnamese documents with triage expert annotations, which materially increases sample size compared to prior Vietnamese readability studies.
evidence: Section 3.1 and Table 1 showing final N=996 with category counts (235, 413, 348).
Prior Vietnamese studies cited had 20 and 54 documents (Nguyen & Henkin 1982/1985).

strengths.title: Clear, interpretable feature definitions and simple final formula
strengths.description: Features (ASLC, AWLC, PDW) are precisely defined with equations and the final linear formula is explicit and easy to compute or replicate.
evidence: Feature equations (8-14) define ASLC, AWLC, PDW; Equation 16 presents final formula with numeric coefficients.
Table 3 lists fold-level coefficients, enabling reproducibility.

strengths.title: Cross-fold reporting and per-class accuracy breakdown
strengths.description: The study performs 5-fold cross-validation and reports fold-wise and averaged per-class and overall accuracies, which helps evaluate variability across folds.
evidence: Table 3 lists per-fold accuracies for Easy/Normal/Difficult and Overall and reports average coefficients across folds.

concerns.title: Annotation reliability insufficiently characterized
concerns.description: Fleiss' kappa is reported as 0.422 (moderate agreement) but no further per-item, per-annotator distributions, confidence intervals, or analyses of systematic disagreement are provided. This leaves uncertainty about label noise, boundary ambiguity between classes, and how much the model may be learning annotator inconsistency rather than stable readability signals.
evidence: Section 3.1 reports kappa = 0.422 and describes 3-rater protocol but no other annotation diagnostics or sample disagreements.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-document annotation counts, confusion matrices of rater pairs, kappa confidence intervals (bootstrap), examples of disagreed documents, and optionally an adjudication process or majority-consensus analysis to quantify label noise and its impact on model training.

concerns.title: Potential circularity in PDW2 (corpus-derived easy list)
concerns.description: PDW2, the percentage of difficult words computed using a top-1,000 frequent-word list extracted from the corpus' 'easy' documents, is used as a predictor on the same corpus. This risks circularity: the feature may capture corpus-specific artifacts and overfit, inflating within-corpus performance and harming generalization.
evidence: Section 3.2 defines PDW2 as top-1000 words from easy documents; Table 2 shows PDW2 correlation with TR = 0.786; discussion acknowledges PDW1 (newspaper) correlates poorly.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablation experiments replacing PDW2 with PDW1 and with PDW lists extracted from held-out external corpora; report model performance differences. Also evaluate the formula on an external dataset or leave-one-genre-out folds where PDW2 is computed without using test-fold documents (strict separation) to test for circularity.

concerns.title: Ad-hoc feature selection and multicollinearity handling
concerns.description: Feature selection uses a sequential correlation ranking with a 0.9 pairwise-correlation removal threshold. This heuristic lacks justification and more formal multicollinearity diagnostics (e.g., VIF) or model selection (regularization, stepwise AIC/BIC, or cross-validated feature selection) are not reported.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes selection threshold 0.9 and Table 2 shows high inter-feature correlations (e.g., ASLS-ASLC=0.997, AWLS-AWLC=0.979, ASLC-AWLC=0.716).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute VIFs for chosen features and candidate sets; consider LASSO or ridge regression and compare coefficient stability; report sensitivity of final coefficients and accuracy to feature subset choices.

concerns.title: Lack of inferential statistics and model diagnostics
concerns.description: The paper reports averaged coefficients across folds but provides no standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values, residual analyses, or checks of OLS assumptions (linearity, homoscedasticity, residual normality). Without these, the statistical significance and stability of coefficients are unknown.
evidence: Table 3 gives only raw coefficient values per fold and averages; no SEs or diagnostic plots/tables are provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report coefficient standard errors and t-statistics (or bootstrap CIs), provide residual plots and tests for heteroscedasticity, and document whether transformations or interaction terms were considered.

concerns.title: Unexamined rounding strategy for mapping continuous predictions to classes
concerns.description: Predicted continuous readability scores are rounded to the nearest integer to obtain discrete class labels. The paper does not analyze boundary calibration, alternative ordinal models, or whether thresholds align with annotator behavior — this operational choice can distort class-level accuracy and hide model calibration issues.
evidence: Section 3.3: 'The predicted values were rounded to the nearest unit...' and Table 3 shows resulting per-class accuracies; no analysis of thresholds or alternatives provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report distribution of predicted continuous scores per true class, analyze errors near class boundaries, compare rounding to optimally-chosen thresholds, and evaluate ordinal regression or direct multiclass classifiers as baselines.

concerns.title: No external/out-of-domain validation for generalizability
concerns.description: All reported performance metrics come from within-corpus 5-fold CV. There is no held-out external dataset or domain-separated folds (e.g., by source/genre) to measure how the formula generalizes to unseen text types.
evidence: Cross-validation is described as five equal parts within the corpus; no external testing or domain-separated analysis is reported; discussion acknowledges need for future domain-specific corpora.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate the formula on held-out texts from different sources or genres not used in training (or perform leave-one-source-out CV), and report performance using PDW lists computed without access to test-domain easy lists.

concerns.title: Overstated practical applicability without portability tests
concerns.description: Authors claim the formula can be applied in practice; however, portability depends on availability/transferability of the corpus-derived PDW2 list and on robustness across genres and time. These practical dependencies are not empirically tested.
evidence: Conclusion: 'This is a good result and can be applied in practice.' while PDW2 is corpus-derived and no portability experiments are reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Temporarily temper practical-application claims or add experiments showing performance when PDW2 is replaced by external lists or when the formula is applied to external datasets.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct earlier Vietnamese readability formulas and corpora (small N).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Earlier Vietnamese formulas used small corpora (20 and 54 docs) and surface features (word/sentence length); current paper increases corpus size and re-evaluates surface features with PDW derived from corpus.
comparable_works.source_trace: Paper references (Nguyen and Henkin, 1982; 1985) and Related Works section.

comparable_works.citation_label: Dale-Chall; Flesch; Flesch-Kincaid; Gunning Fog; SMOG
comparable_works.relevance: Classic linear readability formulas for English that motivate feature choices (sentence length, syllable/word difficulty).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Methodologically similar (linear formula, simple surface features) but use syllable/word lists and separate grade-level scales; Vietnamese orthography and morphology mean direct porting may not be optimal.

comparable_works.relevance: External Vietnamese frequent-word lists used as baseline PDW1 in the study.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: PDW1 derived from newspaper corpora; authors find it correlates poorly with readability on their dataset compared to PDW2.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3.2 and Table 2; references to Dinh and Hao (2015).

comparable_works.relevance: Guidelines recommend thorough statistical reporting, validation, and non-hallucinated references; used here to flag missing diagnostics and external validation.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Not a prior research work but reviewer-guideline context indicating expected reporting standards.

uncertainty_flags: Moderate inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa = 0.422) casts doubt on label reliability and effective target signal.
PDW2 is derived from the same corpus (easy documents) producing possible circularity in feature construction and evaluation.
No inferential statistics for regression coefficients, nor residual diagnostics, hide uncertainty about model validity.
Rounding continuous scores to integer classes is an untested operational choice and could distort reported accuracies.
Cross-validation is within a single corpus with mixed sources; domain leakage or source-based clustering could inflate CV performance.
alternative_interpretations: High within-corpus correlation and CV accuracy may partly reflect genre- or source-specific cues (e.g., length and vocabulary style of textbooks vs. news vs. legal texts) rather than generalizable readability signals.

PDW2's strong correlation could indicate that the 'easy' subset contains highly stylized vocabulary (e.g., child-focused lexicon) that is distinctive in this corpus; the model may be learning these idiosyncratic markers instead of general word difficulty.

Moderate kappa suggests annotators diverge frequently on borderline texts; model accuracy could be high simply because the formula captures the majority-class tendencies rather than nuanced human judgments.
Character-based measures may proxy for document length or formatting differences (e.g., inclusion of lists, headings) that coincide with difficulty labels rather than true linguistic difficulty.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides raw counts and per-fold coefficients/accuracies but omits standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals, and per-document annotation data that are necessary to fully evaluate statistical claims.
PDW2 construction method (top-1000 words from easy docs) is described, but the exact extracted list is not provided; sharing it would aid replication and portability tests.

Cross-validation protocol is described at a high level but the randomization stratification scheme (if any), seed, and whether PDW2 was recomputed per fold are not specified; clarifying these is important to rule out information leakage.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The approach—building a substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus and deriving a compact linear formula using character-length measures and a corpus-derived easy-word list—appears to have sparse close analogs in Vietnamese NLP literature and so may be novel. However, novelty does not imply empirical validity: the risk of circularity and limited statistical reporting must be addressed before practical claims.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If PDW2 is recomputed only on training folds and the formula still achieves similar CV performance, the circularity concern is mitigated and the method is likely robust.

If annotator agreement can be improved or shown to be reliable for majority labels (e.g., after adjudication or by reporting item-wise agreement), then the corpus provides a sound ground truth and the model's performance is meaningful.
If external validation on held-out domains (news, legal texts, textbooks) shows comparable accuracy, the formula can be considered portable and practically useful.
If coefficient significance (bootstrap CIs) confirms non-zero effects and residual diagnostics show no major OLS violations, the linear model choice is supported.

novelty_lenses.verdict: plausibly novel within Vietnamese readability work but incremental relative to general readability literature
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper scales prior Vietnamese work by an order of magnitude in corpus size and produces an explicit linear formula, but the method (surface features + linear regression) follows long-established readability practices from English and other languages.
evidence: Prior Vietnamese studies used very small corpora (20 and 54 docs) while this corpus has 996 docs.
Use of sentence/word length and percentage difficult words is conventional in readability research (e.g., Dale-Chall, Flesch).
uncertainty_flags: Claims about being 'new' should be couched: the dataset scale is new for Vietnamese but methodological novelty is modest.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The conceptual move (corpus-derived PDW list for PDW feature) is interesting but risks circularity; the modeling approach is simple and does not introduce fundamentally new algorithmic paradigms.
evidence: PDW2 is an adaptation of 'easy word list' idea but derived from corpus rather than external lexicon; no new learning algorithm or representation is proposed.
uncertainty_flags: If PDW2 were shown to generalize across corpora, the idea could be more disruptive; currently evidence is limited.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am fairly confident (high) that the paper's reported within-corpus numbers (coefficients, fold accuracies) accurately reflect the experiments described in the manuscript. However, I assign moderate-to-low confidence that the reported formula will generalize to other Vietnamese corpora or that the chosen features are sufficient across domains, due to issues around annotation reliability, PDW2 circularity, and absent statistical diagnostics. The numeric interval (0.15-0.85) encodes uncertainty about external validity and the strength of broader claims.

consensus_findings: The paper assembles a substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus (final N = 996) than prior local work and documents sources and basic corpus statistics.

Simple surface features (average sentence length in characters ASLC, average word length in characters AWLC, and a percent-difficult-words PDW computed from a corpus-derived 'easy' list) correlate strongly with the human-assigned readability labels in the assembled corpus.

A small linear regression using ASLC, AWLC and PDW2 fitted with 5-fold cross-validation and whose continuous outputs are rounded to discrete classes attains roughly 81% overall accuracy on internal CV folds as reported by the authors.
The corpus-derived frequent-word list (PDW2) shows far stronger correlation with the corpus' readability labels than an external newspaper-derived list (PDW1) in the reported correlation analyses.

Multiple reviewers identify consistent methodological/reporting gaps: moderate inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa = 0.422) is reported but not deeply analyzed; feature-selection and multicollinearity are handled with an ad-hoc correlation threshold; regression coefficients are reported without inferential statistics or residual diagnostics; PDW2 risks circularity; and no external or domain-separated validation is reported.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: some reviewers treat the work as a meaningful, practically useful incremental contribution because of the much larger Vietnamese corpus and language-specific feature choices; others emphasize that methodologically it largely adapts classic readability ideas and so is not conceptually disruptive. (Controlled difference: novelty-as-resource vs novelty-as-method.)

Severity of practical-applicability claim: several reviewers view the reported ~81% as a plausible in-corpus result but argue it is overstated for deployment without external validation; a minority emphasize the result's immediate pragmatic utility if users accept the corpus-derived PDW. (Difference centers on willingness to accept PDW2 portability.)

Interpretation of Fleiss' kappa = 0.422: all agree this is 'moderate', but reviewers differ in how fatal they view that to the study's validity — some recommend immediate further annotation analyses/adjudication while others consider the corpus still useful provided label-noise is addressed in follow-up analyses.
uncertainty_hotspots: PDW2 circularity and domain leakage: PDW2 is extracted from the corpus' easy subset and then used as a predictor on the same corpus; it is unclear whether PDW2's strong effect generalizes beyond the collected documents or is an artifact of dataset-specific vocabulary.

Annotation quality and label noise: Fleiss' kappa = 0.422 (moderate agreement) is reported without confidence intervals, per-item annotator vote matrices, or analyses of where disagreements concentrate (genres, lengths, borderline items). The extent to which label noise affects model estimates is unknown.

Feature-selection and multicollinearity: selection used a heuristic pairwise correlation cutoff (0.9) rather than formal diagnostics (VIF, condition index) or regularized/model-based selection; coefficient stability under multicollinearity is unquantified.

Statistical inference missing: coefficients are reported as point estimates averaged over folds but without standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals or residual diagnostics (linearity, homoscedasticity, influential points). Hypothesis strength for each predictor is therefore uncertain.

Prediction-to-class mapping: rounding continuous regression outputs to nearest integer is operationally simple but unexamined; there is no analysis of boundary errors, predicted-score distributions by true class, nor comparison to ordinal or direct multiclass models.

Generalizability/out-of-domain robustness: all reported evaluation is within-corpus 5-fold CV. There is no held-out external dataset or leave-one-genre/source-out analysis to estimate portability across text types and time.
model_diversity_effects: Structure_analyst (logical-coherence-first) accentuated argument-chain gaps: he highlighted how missing diagnostics break inference links (annotation -> model -> claim about applicability). This role surfaces where the chain of reasoning needs repair.

Methodology_auditor (reproducibility-first) focused on reproducibility and validation mechanics: requests for annotation matrices, code, exact preprocessing/tokenization, fold-level PDW recomputation, and VIF/SE/residual reporting reflect this lens and raise tests that will most impact reproducibility.

Novelty_assessors (incremental and disruptive lenses) treated the corpus as the primary novelty signal. They flagged that sparse prior Vietnamese resources make the dataset and formula potentially valuable while simultaneously cautioning that methodological gaps (PDW circularity, missing diagnostics) critically affect whether novelty yields a robust, generalizable advance.

Claim_verifier emphasized evidence-for-claims: accepts that reported numbers accurately reflect in-corpus experiments but stresses that extrapolative claims (sufficiency, practical applicability across domains) lack supporting evidence.

Net effect: role diversity preserves controlled disagreement — reviewers converge on the empirical fact pattern (what was done, what numbers were reported) but diverge on interpretation and implications. Methodological reviewers push for more rigorous validation; novelty reviewers see resource value even if further validation is required.
meta_review.editor_guidance:
As editor, the next requested actions should prioritize analyses that directly resolve the main uncertainty hotspots and enable reproducibility. Suggested mandatory revisions and evidence to request from authors (ordered by importance):

1) Annotation transparency and label-quality analysis: provide the anonymized per-document annotation matrix (three annotator votes per doc), counts of filtered documents, bootstrap/confidence intervals for Fleiss' kappa, per-class marginal distributions, and a confusion analysis of annotator disagreements. If possible, report results on a high-agreement subset or perform adjudication for ambiguous items and show sensitivity of model results to label filtering.

2) PDW circularity controls: clarify whether PDW2 was recomputed per CV training fold or computed once on full corpus. If not done per fold, authors must recompute PDW2 using only training data in each fold (no test leakage) and re-run CV. Additionally, provide an ablation where PDW2 is replaced by PDW1 (Dinh & Hao) and report the impact on accuracy and coefficients; if feasible, construct PDW lists from held-out external 'easy' texts and evaluate.

3) Multicollinearity and selection robustness: report VIFs or condition numbers for chosen predictors, compare to alternative selection methods (LASSO or stepwise AIC/BIC) and report whether coefficients and performance materially change. Provide bootstrap or fold-level dispersion measures for coefficients rather than only point averages.

4) Statistical inference and diagnostics: supply standard errors, p-values or bootstrap confidence intervals for coefficients, and residual diagnostics (residual vs fitted, QQ-plot, tests for heteroscedasticity). If OLS assumptions are materially violated, request alternative modeling (robust regression or ordinal models) and comparisons.

5) Prediction mapping and model comparisons: provide distribution plots of predicted continuous scores by true class, confusion matrices and per-class precision/recall/F1, and a direct comparison between regression+rounding vs ordinal logistic regression and at least one multiclass classifier (e.g., logistic regression, random forest) using the same features.

6) Generalization tests: if any independent Vietnamese text collections are available (or by holding out one source/genre), request leave-one-source-out CV or an external test set evaluation to assess portability. If data collection is not feasible, a leave-one-genre/source-out within the current corpus is required.

7) Reproducibility package: require release of code (preprocessing/tokenization rules, exact PDW extraction scripts), PDW lists (PDW2 and PDW1 used), CV splits (random seeds), and the corpus or a clearly documented access policy consistent with privacy/rights.

Ask authors to present the requested analyses clearly and to temper broad applicability claims if new results reduce performance or reveal domain sensitivity. Preserve the editor's central decision-making role: these analyses should be supplied before making publication-level judgments.
meta_review.author_guidance:
To strengthen empirical claims and enable reproducibility, address the following concrete items in a revision and in supplementary materials:

1) Annotation data and analysis: publish the anonymized annotation matrix (3 votes per document), counts and IDs of filtered documents, and compute bootstrapped confidence intervals for Fleiss' kappa. Provide a confusion matrix of annotator votes and examples of high-disagreement items; report results (model fit and accuracy) on a majority-agreed subset to show sensitivity to label noise.

2) PDW construction and leakage control: explicitly state whether PDW2 was computed once on the full corpus or per training fold. Recompute PDW2 inside each CV training fold (strict train/test separation), re-run the 5-fold experiments, and report updated coefficients and accuracies. Run an ablation replacing PDW2 with PDW1 and with PDW lists extracted from an independent easy-text source (or constructed from training folds only) and report downstream performance.

3) Multicollinearity and feature-selection robustness: compute and report VIFs for final and candidate feature sets; perform alternative selection strategies (LASSO with cross-validation, stepwise selection) and report whether feature coefficients and accuracy are stable. If multicollinearity is problematic, consider regularized estimates or dimensionality reduction and report comparison results.

4) Statistical inference and diagnostics: provide standard errors, t-statistics or bootstrap confidence intervals and p-values for coefficients (per-fold and aggregated). Include residual diagnostics (residual vs fitted, QQ-plot) and tests for heteroscedasticity and influential observations; if OLS assumptions fail, present and compare alternative models (robust regression, GLM, ordinal regression).

5) Prediction calibration and class-mapping: show the distribution of continuous predicted scores by true class and analyze how many predictions fall near integer boundaries. Compare regression+rounding to ordinal logistic regression and at least one multiclass classifier (same features) and present confusion matrices, per-class precision/recall/F1 and paired statistical tests (e.g., McNemar) where applicable.

6) Generalizability checks: run leave-one-genre/source-out CV or evaluate on any available external Vietnamese texts not used in training. Report per-domain performance and indicate practical limits of the formula (which domains it performs well on, where PDW must be adapted).

7) Reproducibility artifacts: release code/data needed to reproduce (tokenization/sentence-splitting rules for Vietnamese, PDW extraction scripts, PDW lists, CV splits and random seeds) or provide clear access instructions and licensing for the corpus. Document preprocessing choices that affect character and syllable counts (diacritic handling, punctuation removal, tokenization heuristics).

8) Temper claims where evidence is limited: revise statements about generalized practical applicability to reflect domain dependence and the need for external validation unless the new analyses show robust transfer.

Addressing these points will materially reduce the primary uncertainty sources (annotation quality, PDW circularity, multicollinearity, and absent inference) and substantially strengthen the paper's claims.
transparency_report: Materials provided in the submission that reviewers used: manuscript text, Table 1 (corpus counts/statistics), Table 2 (feature correlations), Table 3 (per-fold coefficients and accuracies), equations defining features and the final formula, and a brief description of annotation protocol and Fleiss' kappa value.

Key items missing or under-specified in the manuscript: per-document annotator votes or aggregated confusion matrices; confidence intervals for Fleiss' kappa; whether PDW2 was computed per training fold or once on full corpus; preprocessing/tokenization and syllable-counting rules (important for character/syllable measures in Vietnamese); code or scripts for PDW extraction and CV splits; standard errors/p-values/CI for regression coefficients and accuracy estimates; residual diagnostics and VIFs; confusion matrices and per-class precision/recall/F1; and any external/leave-one-source-out validation.

Data/code reproducibility status: reviewers could not verify computations because the PDW lists, exact preprocessing, per-document annotations and CV split details were not provided. A reproducibility package is requested (code, PDW lists, CV seeds, and corpus access or an explicit access policy).

Which missing items are highest priority to resolve the core uncertainties: (1) per-fold PDW recomputation (to eliminate PDW2 leakage), (2) annotation matrix and kappa CI (to evaluate label noise), (3) VIFs and coefficient SEs/CI (to evaluate multicollinearity and coefficient reliability), and (4) confusion matrices and per-class metrics (to understand error patterns).
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is based solely on the manuscript and five specialist reviews provided; I did not access raw data, the authors' code, or third-party reproductions. I cannot verify numeric computations, PDW extraction steps, or whether information leakage occurred (e.g., PDW2 recomputed per fold) beyond what was stated. My mapping emphasizes observed claims, reviewer-identified gaps, and recommended analyses to reduce uncertainty, but cannot determine whether re-analyses by the authors would preserve the reported ~81% accuracy or materially change conclusions. Remaining uncertainties include true out-of-domain performance, the degree to which PDW2 effect generalizes versus capturing corpus-specific vocabulary, and the extent to which label noise (kappa=0.422) biases model estimation. The editor should treat this synthesis as evidence-based guidance for targeted revision requests rather than as validation of final claims.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript presents a new Vietnamese readability corpus (final N = 996) labeled by three expert annotators per document (Fleiss' κ = 0.422) and proposes a simple linear Readability formula: Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 − 0.7295. The model uses three surface features (average sentence length in characters, average word length in characters, and percentage of difficult words based on a corpus-derived 'easy' list PDW2), evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation with continuous outputs rounded to integer classes; reported average overall accuracy ≈ 81% (per-class: Easy ≈ 76.6%, Normal ≈ 85.7%, Difficult ≈ 78.5%). Reviewers agree the corpus and interpretable formula are useful contributions but consistently identify methodological and reporting gaps that limit claims about sufficiency and generalizability.
strengths: Substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus (N = 996) than prior local studies, with documented sources and basic corpus statistics.
Clear, interpretable feature definitions and an explicit linear formula using simple, easy-to-compute surface metrics (ASLC, AWLC, PDW).
Cross-fold reporting: per-fold coefficients and per-fold accuracies are provided rather than a single summary point, allowing preliminary assessment of variability across CV splits.
Attention to frequency-list source sensitivity: authors compare corpus-derived PDW2 and an external newspaper-derived list (PDW1) and report markedly different correlation profiles.
limitations: Annotation quality undercharacterized: Fleiss' kappa = 0.422 is reported without confidence intervals, per-item/per-annotator vote matrices, or confusion analyses; label noise and boundary ambiguity are not quantified and may affect model learning.

PDW2 circularity / potential leakage: PDW2 is derived from the corpus' own 'easy' documents; the manuscript does not make explicit whether PDW2 was recomputed per training fold (train-only) during CV. This risks inflated in-corpus performance and reduced out-of-domain validity.

Feature-selection and multicollinearity handled heuristically: selection used a sequential correlation ranking with an ad-hoc 0.9 pairwise-correlation cutoff; no VIFs, condition indices, or regularized-selection comparisons (LASSO/ridge/stepwise) are reported to assess coefficient stability.

Insufficient statistical reporting and diagnostics: regression coefficients are shown as point estimates averaged across folds but lack standard errors, p-values or confidence intervals; no residual diagnostics (linearity, homoscedasticity, influential points) or formal tests of model assumptions are presented.

Prediction-to-class operationalization unexamined: mapping continuous regression outputs to discrete classes by rounding is used without analysis of boundary effects, predicted-score distributions by class, confusion matrices, or comparisons to ordinal/multiclass models.

No external or domain-separated validation: evaluation is limited to within-corpus 5-fold CV, and no leave-one-genre/source-out or independent test set is reported to assess generalizability or domain sensitivity.
open_questions: Was PDW2 (the corpus-derived top-1,000 'easy' words) computed once on the full corpus or recomputed inside each CV training fold? Please describe the exact PDW construction protocol and re-run CV with PDW recomputed from training data only if not already done.

Can the authors provide the anonymized per-document annotation matrix (three annotator votes per document), counts/IDs of filtered documents, and bootstrap/confidence intervals for Fleiss' κ? How do model results change when trained/evaluated on a high-consensus subset?

Please report inferential statistics: per-fold and aggregated standard errors or bootstrap confidence intervals and p-values for coefficients; VIFs or condition numbers for multicollinearity diagnostics; and residual diagnostic plots/tests (e.g., residuals vs fitted, QQ-plot, Breusch–Pagan).

Provide confusion matrices and per-class precision/recall/F1 (per fold and averaged). How do results compare if the task is modeled with ordinal logistic regression or multiclass classifiers using the same features (i.e., alternative to regression+rounding)?

What is the performance when PDW2 is replaced by PDW1 (Dinh & Hao) in the full regression model (not only correlation), and what happens if PDW lists are derived from external easy-text corpora or computed from training folds only (leave-one-domain-out tests)?

Please describe preprocessing/tokenization details used for character/syllable/word counts (diacritic handling, sentence splitting, tie-breaking in frequency lists) and provide code/scripts and PDW lists to enable replication.
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the paper provides a useful, substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus and an interpretable linear formula evaluated with 5-fold CV yielding ~81% in-corpus accuracy.

All reviewers identify the same core methodological/reporting weaknesses: moderate annotator agreement not deeply analyzed; potential PDW2 circularity; ad-hoc feature selection and multicollinearity risks; lack of coefficient uncertainty and residual diagnostics; and no out-of-domain validation.

Reviewers consider the contribution novel in the context of Vietnamese resources (corpus scale and language-specific feature choices) but emphasize that novelty does not substitute for rigorous validation.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of novelty and immediate practical value: some reviewers emphasize the practical value of the corpus and a simple formula (resource-centered novelty), while others caution that PDW2 circularity and missing diagnostics substantially limit practical applicability until resolved (methodology-centered skepticism).

Severity of Fleiss' κ = 0.422: reviewers agree this is 'moderate' but differ on whether this alone invalidates the corpus for modeling (some see it as fixable/reportable; others see it as a major threat requiring adjudication or sensitivity analyses).

Interpretation of PDW2's superiority: some reviewers view the corpus-derived PDW2 as a promising language-specific innovation; others view PDW2's strong correlation as plausibly an artifact of deriving the list from labeled 'easy' texts used during training (i.e., dataset-specific vocabulary signal).
uncertainty_snapshot: Primary uncertainties concern PDW2 circularity (was PDW computed with test-fold data?), the impact of label noise on model estimates (moderate κ), and coefficient stability under multicollinearity.
Secondary uncertainties concern the operational choice of rounding continuous scores to classes and whether observed accuracies would hold under ordinal/multiclass modeling or on external datasets.
Because raw data/code were not available to reviewers, I cannot verify whether any leakage occurred or whether the reported averages hide unstable fold-level behavior beyond the provided tables.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The authors present a near-1,000-document Vietnamese readability corpus and an explicit linear readability formula built from three surface features (ASLC, AWLC, PDW2). Internal 5-fold cross-validation with regression outputs rounded to integer classes yields ~81% average accuracy. The dataset and transparent formula are potentially valuable given sparse prior Vietnamese resources.

Strengths:
- Substantially expands Vietnamese readability resources (N = 996) with documented sources.
- Produces an interpretable, low-cost linear formula using straightforward character-based features and an easy-word percentage.
- Reports per-fold coefficients and accuracies enabling preliminary assessment of variability.

Limitations:
- Annotation reliability not fully characterized: Fleiss' κ = 0.422 reported without CI or per-item/annotator breakdown; label noise and its impact on modeling are not analyzed.
- PDW2 circularity risk: PDW2 is derived from the corpus' easy documents and the manuscript does not clarify whether PDW2 was recomputed in a train-only manner inside CV; this may inflate in-corpus performance and harm generalizability.
- Feature-selection and multicollinearity handled with an ad-hoc 0.9 correlation cutoff; no VIF or regularized-selection comparisons reported, so coefficient stability is uncertain.
- Missing inferential statistics and diagnostics: coefficients lack SEs/p-values/CIs, and no residual diagnostics or formal assumption tests are shown.
- Operational mapping to discrete classes by rounding is unexamined; no confusion matrices or comparisons to ordinal/multiclass models are reported.
- No external or domain-separated validation provided to establish portability across genres or sources.

Open Questions:
1) Was PDW2 computed once on the full corpus or recomputed per training fold? Please clarify and, if needed, rerun CV with PDW recomputed using training data only.
2) Please provide the anonymized annotation matrix (3 votes/doc), κ confidence intervals (bootstrap), and sensitivity analyses (model trained on high-agreement subset). How many items were near-boundary or filtered?
3) Provide standard errors/p-values or bootstrap confidence intervals for coefficients, and VIFs or condition indices for multicollinearity diagnostics. Do coefficients remain stable under LASSO or stepwise selection?
4) Provide confusion matrices and per-class precision/recall/F1, predicted-score distributions by true class, and compare regression+rounding against ordinal logistic regression and a multiclass classifier using the same features.

Transparency:
Reviewers had access to manuscript tables and equations but not to raw annotations, PDW lists, preprocessing/tokenization code, or CV splits. These missing artifacts limit reproducibility and prevent verification of whether PDW2 was computed train-only. The highest-priority missing items are: (a) PDW construction protocol (per-fold vs full-corpus), (b) per-document annotator votes and κ CIs, (c) VIFs and coefficient uncertainty (SEs/CI), and (d) confusion matrices and per-class metrics.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence bounds reflect that reported in-corpus results (coefficients and ~81% CV accuracy) are credible as described, but substantial methodological uncertainties (PDW2 circularity, moderate κ without deeper analysis, missing coefficient/inference diagnostics, and absent external validation) materially widen uncertainty about generalizability and the stronger claims of sufficiency/practical applicability. The lower bound represents the plausible degree to which unresolved circularity and label noise could reduce external validity; the upper bound reflects the observed in-corpus signal and that straightforward remedial analyses could largely validate the contribution.

In a sense text summarization falls also under the category of Natural Language Generation. It helps in figuring out whether or not a lengthy document meets the user’s needs and is worth reading for further information. With large texts, text summarization processes and summarizes the document in the time it would take the user to read the first paragraph. The key to summarization is to reduce the length and detail of a document while retaining its main points and overall meaning. One of the strategies most widely used by text summarization tools is sentence extraction. Important sentences from an article are statistically weighted and ranked. Summarization tools may also search for headings and other markers of subtopics in order to identify the key points of a document. The methods of summarization can be classified in two broad groups: • shallow analysis, restricted to the syntactic level of representation and try to extract significant parts of the text; • deeper analysis, assumes a semantics level of representation of the original text (typically using Information Retrieval techniques). Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

In a sense text summarization falls also under the category of Natural Language Generation. It helps in figuring out whether or not a lengthy document meets the user’s needs and is worth reading for further information. With large texts, text summarization processes and summarizes the document in the time it would take the user to read the first paragraph. The key to summarization is to reduce the length and detail of a document while retaining its main points and overall meaning. One of the strategies most widely used by text summarization tools is sentence extraction. Important sentences from an article are statistically weighted and ranked. Summarization tools may also search for headings and other markers of subtopics in order to identify the key points of a document. The methods of summarization can be classified in two broad groups: • shallow analysis, restricted to the syntactic level of representation and try to extract significant parts of the text; • deeper analysis, assumes a semantics level of representation of the original text (typically using Information Retrieval techniques).
